list.listitem: In a child with a cold, consider rhinosinusitis when symptoms last beyond 10 days or when they are more severe than usual or worsen after several days of improvement. Suspect a complication if orbital or meningeal or neurological symptoms. C
Prescribe antibiotics in cases of severe illness with concomitant high fever and purulent rhinorrhea. B
Consider antibiotics in patients with protracted symptoms. Intranasal corticosteroids may also be considered. B
Hospitalize for IV antibiotic treatment (and/or surgery) in cases of severe illness or toxicity with suspected or proven suppurative complication. C
For children with chronic rhinosinusitis not responsive to medication, adenoidectomy, balloon sinuplasty, and endoscopic sinus surgery are more invasive treatment options.B

background.definition: Sinusitis is an inflammation of the mucosa of the paranasal sinuses usually caused by an infection. As this inflammation also involves the nasal epithelium, rhinosinusitis is the more accurate term.

list.listitem: Children suffer 6 to 8 colds a year, and the sinuses are almost always involved; incidence decreases after 6 to 8 years.
Rhinosinusitis develops with colds in 6% to 13% of children by the age of 3.
In 5% to 10% of sinus infections, a bacterial superinfection occurs.
The incidence of sinusitis is higher in autumn and winter and among children attending day care.
Sinuses may become inflamed from a viral upper respiratory tract infection.
The bacterial infection agent involved may be Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, or Moraxella catarrhalis.
Allergies are associated with an increased risk for chronic rhinosinusitis.
Cystic fibrosis, primary ciliary dyskinesia, and immune deficiencies are uncommon risk factors.
Acute rhinosinusitis is usually triggered by viral upper respiratory tract infection, and almost always the sinuses are also involved.
In 5% to 10% of patients a bacterial superinfection occurs.
Consider rhinosinusitis in children with persistent cold symptoms more than 10 days, a cold that is more severe than usual, or a cold that worsens after initial improvement. C
Suspect a complication in children of eye swelling, exophthalmos, impaired extraocular eye movements, signs of increased intracranial pressure, meningeal irritation, or focal neurologic deficits. C
Imaging is not necessary; CT scans should be reserved for patients in whom surgery is being considered as a management strategy. C

Differential.Differential_Name: Sequential episodes of URTI (upper respiratory tract infection)
Differential.Differential_Features: Differentiation from persistent illness: episode usually shorter (5-7 days). By day 10 complaints are usually subsiding

Differential.Differential_Name: Moderately ill with uncomplicated viral infection
Differential.Differential_Features: Differentiation from severe illness: fever in the first 48 hours, respiratory symptoms appear later. Purulent discharge appears after several days. In severe rhinosinusitis the patient presents concurrent high fever and purulent rhinorrhea
Differentiation from rhinosinusitis: less pain, secretions typically clear, no fever

list.listitem: Acute bacterial sinusitis should be presumptively diagnosed if a child has: (1) persistent nasal discharge or daytime cough more than 10 days with no improvement, (2) worsening course (new or worsening nasal discharge, daytime cough, or fever) after initial improvement, or (3) fever greater than or equal to 39°C and purulent nasal discharge for 3 days.
Acute rhinosinusitis lasts less than 30 days, subacute rhinosinusitis between 30 and 90 days, and chronic rhinosinusitis longer than 90 days.
Recurrent rhinosinusitis is defined as at least three episodes in 6 months or four episodes in a year of symptoms lasting less than 30 days that recur after at least 10 asymptomatic days.

Presenting symptoms of rhinosinusitis in children are rhinorrhea (71%-80%) and cough (50%-80%). In acute rhinosinusitis, fever (50%-60%) and pain (29%-33%) are common. In chronic rhinosinusitis, nasal obstruction (70%-100%), mouth breathing (70%-100%), and ear complaints (recurrent purulent otitis media or OME in 40%-68%) are common.

On physical examination nasal and pharyngeal mucosa are usually erythematous with yellow or greenish purulent rhinorrhea of varying viscosity. Postnasal drip is seen in about 60% of patients, and pus in the middle meatus in 50%.
There is poor concordance among clinical symptoms and signs, radiology, CT-scan, ultrasonography, and sinus puncture.
Consider orbital and peri-orbital cellulitis in children with unilateral periorbital swelling, a rare but serious complication of acute rhinosinusitis in children.

A systematic review found that the prevalence of imaging confirmed rhinosinusitis among children with sinus symptoms ranged from 57% to 79%. The overall clinical impression is the most accurate "test" for bacterial rhinosinusitis, and cacosmia is somewhat helpful when present.

Imaging studies (plain films, CT, MRI or ultrasound) should not be used to distinguish acute bacterial sinusitis from viral URI and are not routinely recommended in children with clinically suspected rhinosinusitis.
Plain X rays: insensitive and of limited usefulness for diagnosis or to guide surgery. X rays correlate poorly with CT scan; they are not recommended for clinical practice.
Transillumination: not useful in children because of increase in thickness of both the soft tissue and the bony vault of the palate.

CT-scanning: not useful because of high incidence of asymptomatic children with CT scan abnormalities. Also, radiation risks and harms are much greater in children than adults. CT-scanning is only recommended in preparation for surgery in chronic rhinosinusitis.
CT with contrast or MRI with contrast should be obtained when a child is suspected of having orbital or central nervous system complications of acute bacterial sinusitis.
A randomized control trial found that in children with acute sinusitis, testing for specific bacteria on presentation may represent a strategy to reduce antibiotic use.

Consider rhinosinusitis in children with signs and symptoms of a cold that persists beyond 10 days (nasal or postnasal discharge of any quality, daytime cough worsening at night), a cold that seems more severe that usual (high fever, concurrent copious purulent discharge, periorbital edema and pain), or a cold that after several days of improvement worsens with or without fever.

Signs of complication include orbital infection: eye swelling, exophthalmos, impaired extraocular eye movements, signs of increased intracranial pressure, meningeal irritation, and focal neurologic deficits.
Prescribe antibiotics in cases of severe acute rhinosinusitis with concomitant high fever and purulent rhinorrhea or worsening course. B

Consider antibiotics in cases of nonsevere acute rhinosinusitis with protracted symptoms (at least 10 days) or offer outpatient observation for up to 3 additional days before prescribing antibiotics. B
First-line antibiotic is amoxicillin 80 to 90 mg/kg/d (divided BID) with or without clavulanate for 10 days. B
Hospitalize for IV antibiotics if severe illness or toxicity in child is suspected or suppurative complication is proved. C
For children with chronic rhinosinusitis not responsive to medication, adenoidectomy, balloon sinuplasty, and endoscopic sinus surgery are more invasive treatment options.B

A meta-analysis of antibiotics for persistent nasal discharge in children concluded that antibiotics given for 10 days reduced the probability of persistence in the short to medium term (NNT 8; 95% CI, 5-29). No long-term benefits were documented. Patients in the included studies had symptoms for as little as 10 days to more than 3 months. Two recent RCTs comparing placebo to antibiotics or another therapy confirm the conclusion of this meta-analysis.

A 2024 meta-analysis identified 6 studies with just over 900 participants. They found a significantly higher response rate with antibiotics (77% vs 59%, NNT = 6). The data largely come from a single study, which showed a substantial benefit after a few weeks to using amoxicillin with or without clavulanate to treat children with symptoms of acute sinusitis.
Antibiotic treatment has minimal benefit in children with acute sinusitis without nasopharyngeal bacteria present. The effectiveness of the antibiotic did not depend on the color of nasal discharge.
The selected antibiotic should be effective against Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Moraxella catarrhalis.

A cohort study evaluating efficacy and side effects of amoxicillin-clavulanate compared to amoxicillin found no difference in treatment failure between the two groups. However, gastrointestinal symptoms and yeast infections were more frequent in those treated with amoxicillin-clavulanate.

When antibiotics are indicated, start with amoxicillin (80-90 mg/kg/day divided BID) for 10 days. If the patient is allergic to amoxicillin, and the allergic reaction is not a type 1 hypersensitivity reaction, then cefdinir (14 mg/kg/d in 2 divided doses), cefuroxime (30 mg/kg/d in 2 divided doses), and cefpodoxime (10 mg/kg/d once daily) are options. Cephalosporin skin testing before initiaion of therapy can be considered. In children <2 years of age with severe allergic reactions to penicillin and moderate/severe sinusitis, consider prescribing a combination of clindamycin and cefixime or linezolid monotherapy to cover both resistant S. pneumoniae and H. influenzae. T-sulfamethoxazole and azithromycin are not recommended secondary to high resistance of S. pneumoniae and H. influenzae.

A single 50 mg/kg dose of ceftriaxone (IM or IV) can be used for children who are vomiting, unable to tolerate oral medication, or unlikely to be adherent to the initial doses of antibiotic. Oral antibiotic can then be used to complete the course of therapy if clinical improvement is seen in 24 hours.

If the patient does not improve within 72 hours, has recently been treated with antibiotics, has an illness that is more severe, or attends day care, initiate therapy with high-dose amoxicillin-clavulanate (80-90 mg/kg/d of amoxicillin component, 6, 4 mg/kg/d of clavulanate in 2 divided doses). Alternatives are cefdinir, cefuroxime, and cefpodoxime.
Optimal length of antibiotic therapy is a minimum of 10 days, with suggestion of continuing antibiotic therapy for 7 days after the patient becomes symptom-free.

A RCT showed decreased antibiotic prescribing for acute respiratory tract infections when pediatric care providers were given training on best practices and communications regarding antibiotics stewardship in addition to individualized antibiotic prescribing feedback reports.

In the telemedicine setting, a RCT showed decreased antibiotic prescribing for acute respiratory tract infections when providers received both education and individualized feedback. Antibiotic prescriptions for all conditions (URI, bronchitis, sinusitis, pharyngitis) decreased in the post-intervention period compared with those in the pre-intervention period, for both control and intervention groups.
Nasal wash with isotonic saline can help eliminate nasal secretions and can decrease nasal edema.

There is no evidence from clinical trials that topical or oral decongestants, decongestant-antihistamine combinations, or topical/systemic antifungals are effective for rhinosinusitis in children, and they are not recommended.
A Cochrane review of intranasal corticosteroids concluded that they have a modest benefit for acute rhinosinusitis in adults and children and in acute recurrent rhinosinusitis.

An RCT of oral methylprednisolone (1 mg/kg x 10 days, then 0.75 mg/kg x 2 days, then 0.5 mg/kg x 2 days, then 0.25 mg/kg x 1 day) versus placebo, in addition to antibiotics, in children with chronic rhinosinutis (>3 months) concluded that adjuvant methylprednisolone was associated with clinically relevant improvement of symptoms (77% vs. 30%; NNT 2) and CT resolution of sinusitis (86% vs. 52%). Incidence of clinical relapses of sinusitis was not significantly different (25% vs. 43%).

A trial randomized 66 children with chronic rhinosinusitis to intranasal mometasone once daily for 12 weeks plus intranasal saline spray, or saline spray only. The group receiving the corticosteroid had a greater improvement in the SN-5 sinus specific quality of life score (-0.58 points difference, p = 0.009). This difference is of questionable clinical significance though.

A systematic review identified 8 studies with 477 individuals who had orbital complications related to chronic rhinosinusitis (all ages). Systemic steroids were associated with a shorter length of stay (2.9 days) but no difference in the need for surgery.

Less invasive options for children with chronic rhinosinusitis not responsive to medications include adenoidectomy and balloon sinuplasty, which are recommended by guidelines. Adenoidectomy improves symptoms in about half of pediatric patients with chronic rhinosinusitis and is the initial invasive procedure recommended by guidelines.

Absolute indications for pediatric endoscopic sinus surgery (PESS): complete nasal obstruction in cystic fibrosis due to massive polyposis or due to medialization of the lateral nasal wall, orbital abscess, intracranial complications, antrochoanal polyps, mucoceles or mucopyocele, or fungal rhinosinusitis.
Possible indications for PESS: chronic rhinosinusitis with frequent exacerbations that persist despite optimal medical management and after exclusion of any systemic disease.
There is no evidence that endoscopic sinus surgery is superior to medical treatment with or without sinus irrigation in patients with chronic rhinosinusitis.
A small study in children with chronic rhinosinusitis showed no difference in effectiveness between saline and bromhexine by nebulizer.
A Cochrane review found that nasal saline irrigation help improve symptoms of chronic rhinosinusitus.
Another study of 30 children found that hypertonic saline nasal irrigation improved symptoms more than normal saline irrigation.

A retrospective cohort study of 104 children with chronic rhinosinusitis found that nasal irrigation for 6 weeks was associated with 58% of patients reporting resolution of symptoms. No control group reported.

A RCT of adults found that in patients with chronic sinus symptoms, patients using nasal irrigation had improved symptoms at 6 months using the Rhinosinusitis Disability Index, NNT 13; however, there was no difference using the SNOT-20 score. Steam inhalation had no benefit.

A randomized, open-label study of 50 adult patients with mild to moderate acute bacterial rhinosinusitis (ABRS) compared 10 days of Pelargonium sidoides root extract with 10 days of amoxicillin and showed better improvement of ABRS symptoms in those treated with Pelargonium extract.

A systematic review of RCTs evaluating the safety and efficacy of probiotics in adults with chronic sinusitis found the most common side effects to be epistaxis and abdominal pain while showing no reduction in Sino-Nasal Outcome Tests values or reduction of severe symptom frequency. Symptom relapse was lower. The optimal mode, treatment duration, and appropriate patient for probiotic treatment requires further study. Studies in children are needed.
Consider hospitalization for any child with severe illness or toxic appearance, and when suppurative complications are suspected or proved.
Consider IV administration of an agent effective against penicillin-resistant Streptococcus pneumoniae, beta-lactamase producing Haemophilus influenzae, and Moraxella catarrhalis.
Consider pediatric endoscopic sinus surgery in cases of intracranial complications or orbital abcess.
In children 5% to 10% of upper respiratory tract infections are complicated by acute rhinosinusitis. This usually cures spontaneously in less that 30 days. B
Subacute and chronic rhinosinusitis in children is also self-limited. After 6 to 8 years of age the prevalence of rhinosinusitis decreases. B
Complications are very rare. They consist of orbital infection or intracranial abscesses. B
